section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department correspondence and records concerning American motion picture interests and newsreel activities in Japan between 1929 and 1939, with archival charge-outs through 1952. The documents detail representations by the American Motion Picture Association of Japan protesting stringent import quotas, foreign exchange controls, and frozen royalty remittances under the 1939 Motion Picture Law, alongside the Japanese Foreign Office's refusal to license the film 'Gunga Din' following protests by the Indian community. The section also includes early 1932 records and a telegram from Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes concerning a Fox Movietone newsreel interview with Japanese Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai addressing Manchurian pacification and territorial policies toward Manchuria and Mongolia.

subfiles.about: A representation from the American Motion Picture Association of Japan requesting diplomatic assistance regarding Japanese film import restrictions, impending quota cuts under the new Motion Picture Law, and frozen royalty funds.
subfiles.from: American Motion Picture Association of Japan (R. D. Spierman, Hon. Secretary)
keywords: American Motion Picture Association of Japan
subfiles.summary: The American Motion Picture Association of Japan sets forth its difficulties under Japanese exchange and import regulations, noting that while remittance permits for ¥3,000,000 were eventually granted, import permits for the remaining $10,000 in print costs remain stalled. The association contrasts these restrictions with the heavy and unrestricted volume of Japanese film exports to the United States. It expresses deep apprehension regarding the new Motion Picture Law taking effect in January 1940, which threatens severe distribution quotas for American distributors. Finally, noting approximately ¥4,000,000 in accumulated frozen funds, the association appeals to Ambassador Grew for diplomatic intervention and notes coordinated approaches to the Hays Organization and the State Department.
subfiles.title: Representation from the American Motion Picture Association of Japan to Ambassador Grew Concerning Import Restrictions and Frozen Funds
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan

subfiles.about: An official communication from the Japanese Department of Finance establishing terms and conditions for American motion picture imports under credit and royalty remittances.
subfiles.from: Kojiro Nakamura, Head of Exchange Bureau, Department of Finance
subfiles.summary: Kojiro Nakamura informs Michael M. Bergher of the conditional approval of American motion picture imports under credit arranged through promoter Hisaji Kubo. The agreement permits imports up to $30,000 in print costs before the end of 1938 at a minimum cost of 1.5 cents per foot, subject to monthly approval and exchange control ordinances. Royalties up to ¥3,000,000 may be remitted through the Yokohama Specie Bank and converted into U.S. dollars, but must be deposited without interest at the bank's San Francisco branch for three full years before payment can be made to the distributors.
subfiles.title: Department of Finance Terms and Conditions for American Motion Picture Importation and Royalty Remittances
subfiles.to: Michael M. Bergher, Representative of American Motion Picture Association of Japan

subfiles.summary: This Department of State charge-out slip (Form DS-933) tracks file loans and charge-out requests. It records documents and jackets under decimal classifications 800.515/4-1846 and 894.4061 charged out to department offices or personnel in February and March 1952.
subfiles.title: Department of State Document Charge-Out Record (Form DS-933)

subfiles.about: A telegram from Ambassador Grew reporting that Japanese authorities decided to deny an exhibition license for the American film 'Gunga Din'.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that the Embassy made informal representations to the Foreign Office on behalf of RKO Moving Picture Distributors due to significant American financial interests involved. The Japanese Foreign Office officially decided to refuse an exhibition license for 'Gunga Din' on the grounds of adverse reactions in India and protests from the local Indian community. Grew adds that the British Embassy lodged a political protest against the refusal and notes that the American Embassy has exhausted every possible effort to assist the distributors.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 701 Regarding License Refusal for Motion Picture 'Gunga Din'

subfiles.about: A letter from Assistant Secretary of State Messersmith informing Will H. Hays of the Japanese government's refusal to license the exhibition of 'Gunga Din'.
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, United States Assistant Secretary of State
keywords: Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State George S. Messersmith transmits to Will H. Hays the contents of Tokyo's telegram No. 701 of December 23, 1939. He explains that Japanese authorities refused an exhibition license for 'Gunga Din' because of adverse reaction to the film in India. Messersmith assures Hays that the American Embassy in Tokyo did everything within its power to assist the distributors.
subfiles.title: Letter from Assistant Secretary of State Messersmith to Will H. Hays Regarding 'Gunga Din'
subfiles.to: Will H. Hays, President, Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America, Inc.

subfiles.about: A cross-reference note indicating that Telegram No. 3 regarding Premier Inukai's Movietone introduction is filed under decimal number 793.94/3441.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note cross-references Telegram No. 3 sent from Japan by Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes on January 8, 1932. The telegram concerns the Fox Movietone introduction of Japanese Premier Tsuyoshi Inukai to the American public and directs researchers to the main decimal file 793.94/3441.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Cross-Referencing Telegram No. 3 Regarding Premier Inukai's Movietone Introduction

subfiles.about: A telegram reporting on a Fox Movietone filming with Premier Inukai and detailing diplomatic conversations on Japanese military policy in Manchuria and Mongolia.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes reports that he and Edwin L. Neville posed with Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai for a Fox Movietone newsreel introducing Inukai to the American public, during which Inukai declared peace restored in Manchuria. In conversation prior to filming, Forbes followed up on Inukai's previous proposal to provide employment for disbanded Chinese soldiers to curb banditry. Forbes also questioned Inukai regarding General Jiro Minami's aggressive public assertions of Japanese dominance over Manchuria and Mongolia; Inukai clarified that Japan's references applied to Eastern Inner Mongolia and disclaimed designs on Outer Mongolia, while laughing that Manchuria's borders were indeterminate.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 3 Concerning Fox Movietone Interview with Premier Inukai and Manchurian Policy
